statement.p: A car initially going 55 ft/sec brakes at a constant rate (constant negative acceleration), coming to a stop in 4 seconds.
Graph the velocity for t=0 to t=4. How far does the car travel before stopping?
How far does the car travel before stopping if its initial velocity is doubled, but it brakes at the same constant rate?

static.solution:
(Click on the graph for a larger version.)
The distance traveled is just the area under the curve, so the distance is is d= \frac12 (4)(55) = 110.
If the car starts off traveling twice the original velocity of 55, but decelerates at the same rate, we have the graph
(Click on the graph for a larger version.)
(In this, the blue curve is the new velocity graph, while the thinner black curve is the original.) As before, we have d= \frac12 (8) (110) = 440. Note that doubling the initial speed results in multiplying the required distance by four.
